author: Athenagoras of Athens
translation: B. P. Pratten (ANF vol. 2), public domain
note: c. AD 177 — Father, Son, and Holy Spirit named together, 'their power in union and their distinction in order,' nearly 150 years before Nicaea. The 'distinction in order' (taxis) language is the ancient order-of-relation vocabulary, not a claim of inequality; it is orthodox and pre-creedal. Filed under Trinity. Verified verbatim against source_url (apologia-citations, web, 2026-08-24).
text: Who, then, would not be astonished to hear men who speak of God the Father, and of God the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and who declare both their power in union and their distinction in order, called atheists?

author: Athenagoras of Athens
work: On the Resurrection of the Dead
translation: B. P. Pratten (ANF vol. 2), public domain
note: The classic patristic argument from creation to resurrection: the God who first shaped the body from formless matter can raise it again. c. AD 177. Adds depth to the thin Resurrection bucket. NOTE: Athenagoran authorship of On the Resurrection of the Dead is debated in modern scholarship (Grant questioned it; Barnard defends it); ANF prints it as his, and it is 2nd–3rd c. either way. Filed under Resurrection, so it does not feed the deity-of-Christ pre-Nicaea stat. Verified verbatim against source_url (apologia-citations, web, 2026-08-24).
text: For that power which could give shape to what is regarded by them as shapeless matter, and adorn it, when destitute of form and order, with many and diverse forms, and gather into one the several portions of the elements, and divide the seed which was one and simple into many, and organize that which was unorganized, and give life to that which had no life—that same power can reunite what is dissolved, and raise up what is prostrate, and restore the dead to life again, and put the corruptible into a state of incorruption.
